name: Counter-Positioning

positioning.oneLineSummary: Tests whether a superior newcomer business model imposes enough economic self-harm to make a named incumbent rationally delay imitation.
positioning.productLabel: Counter-Positioning Lens — based on Hamilton Helmer's public 7 Powers materials
notAClaimOf: incumbents always being irrational or slow
the mechanism blocking other new entrants

attribution.display: Based on Hamilton Helmer's public Counter-Positioning doctrine

neutralParaphrase: Counter-Positioning may exist when a newcomer adopts a superior business model but a specific incumbent would damage existing profits, channels, assets, organization, incentives, or stakeholder relationships by copying it. The Barrier is incumbent-specific and may buy time; it does not by itself stop another entrant from adopting the same model.

locator.value: Counter-Positioning section lines 173-220: superior model, incumbent damage, organizational and channel conflicts

Foreword lines 37-41: Hastings on rational incumbent behavior and Counter-Positioning

requiredConditions: The newcomer model is superior for a defined customer task.
At least one named incumbent has material existing economics or assets at risk.
Imitation damage is quantified rather than described as culture alone.
Potential entrants and fast followers are evaluated separately.

requiredEvidence.description: Measured customer-value, cost, access, speed, convenience, or quality improvement from the newcomer model.
Revenue, margin, channel, asset, compensation, contract, regulatory, or organizational damage the incumbent would incur by matching.
Observed response, delay, half-measures, cannibalization tolerance, acquisition, or separate-unit strategy.
Other entrants' ability to copy the model and any second Power needed for durable protection.

decisionQuestions: Which incumbent is constrained and what exact economic engine is threatened?
How much value would imitation destroy before replacement economics scale?
Can the incumbent ring-fence, acquire, subsidize, or launch separately?
Has the incumbent delayed for economic reasons rather than simple execution failure?
How long is the likely response window?
What prevents other entrants from copying the newcomer?
positiveSignals: The newcomer offers measured customer superiority with a structurally different model.
Incumbent imitation would cannibalize a large profit pool or strand material assets.
Public actions show delay, conflicted pricing, channel resistance, or incomplete imitation.
The delay window lets the newcomer build another defensible mechanism.
New entrant replication is limited by an independent Barrier.
redFlags: The incumbent is called stupid, old, or bureaucratic without an economic model.
The new product is cheaper only because of temporary subsidy.
Incumbents already copied without material damage.
The model is easy for other startups to reproduce.
A disruption narrative is treated as synonymous with Counter-Positioning.
disconfirmingEvidence: The incumbent can migrate customers while preserving economics.
A separate brand, channel, or business unit avoids collateral damage.
The incumbent willingly cannibalizes and responds rapidly.
Customer superiority vanishes when subsidy or regulation normalizes.
Fast followers adopt the same model and compete away returns.
contraindications: Do not diagnose management irrationality when economic self-harm is not shown.
Do not treat this as a barrier against all entrants.
Do not assume the response window is permanent.

instructions: Define the newcomer model and measured customer superiority.
Model imitation economics for each named incumbent.
Compare predicted and observed incumbent response.
Assess fast followers, substitutes, and the need for a second Power.
Conclude on the existence and likely duration of Counter-Positioning.

sourceReliability.low: Only a founder disruption narrative is available.
sourceReliability.medium: Incumbent public economics and some response evidence are available.
sourceReliability.high: Reconciled incumbent economics, customer evidence, and observed response converge.

evidenceStrength.low: No material incumbent self-harm is quantified.
evidenceStrength.medium: Self-harm is material but response paths or entrants remain uncertain.
evidenceStrength.high: Economic damage predicts observed delay and a durable follow-on Barrier exists.

evidenceCoverage.low: New model or incumbent economics are missing.
evidenceCoverage.medium: Superiority and incumbent damage are covered but entrants are incomplete.
evidenceCoverage.high: Customer value, damage, response options, time window, entrants, and decay are covered.

applicabilityConfidence.low: There is no established incumbent economic engine.
applicabilityConfidence.high: The opportunity directly attacks a material incumbent profit or asset base.

judgmentConfidence.low: Only a disruption label is supported.
judgmentConfidence.high: Material self-harm, observed delay, and the response window are well supported.

promotionRequirements: Backtest predicted incumbent responses using decision-date evidence.
Validate treatment of fast followers and second-Power requirements.
empiricalQualifications: Retrospective narratives can mistake failed execution for rational self-harm.
Incumbents can use acquisitions, separate units, or cannibalization to respond.
The mechanism is often temporary and incumbent-specific.

rights.notes: Public interview doctrine and official foreword are neutrally paraphrased.
